subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FLOOR PRICES ON CATTLE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FLOOR PRICES ON CATTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as recently
announced in parliament, the federal government has agreed to establish a floor price on cattle until the United States embargo on Canadian cattle and beef shipments is removed. This price, until July, will be on the basis of $25 per hundredweight for good steers at Toronto, Montreal and Moncton; $23.35 at Winnipeg; $22.80 at Saskatoon; $22.55 at Edmonton and Calgary, and $23.40 at Vancouver. At the beginning of June a floor price for the month of July will be announced, and at the beginning of each month thereafter the floor price for the next month will be announced in order that the producer may know what the floor price on his cattle will be for the next two months.
In 1951 Canada exported about 400,000 head of cattle, either as cattle or beef, for which no outside market is at present available although it is hoped that domestic consumption will increase with the lower consumer prices for beef. If the market is oversupplied, it means the price to producers will remain at the floor. With the fixing of a floor price, it will be possible for the producer to market his cattle in an orderly manner with only finished cattle reaching the market, and if this is done the producer may expect to continue to sell all his cattle without undue market gluts, and may from time to time receive prices higher than the floor.
There are various reasons why it will be in the best interests of the cattle industry to delay the marketing of cattle while the
United States embargo is still in effect, and attention is drawn specifically to the following:
1.	When the American embargo is lifted, that market will again be available.
2.	Orderly marketing will relieve market congestion and undue pressure on prices received by farmers.
3.	The establishment of a floor price means the producer will always be in a position to obtain a minimum price for the particular grade of animals which he has to market until such time as the United States embargo is lifted. It is possible that the extra feeding, with the resulting weight gain, may improve the grade and therefore increase returns to the producer.
4.	During the pasture season, cattle make their most economical gains on grass, and this is available on most farms and also in community pastures in western Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
I am sorry to be required to announce that we have one more case of foot-and-mouth disease. The case was first reported on Saturday, April 19, and veterinarians visited the premises immediately and quarantined them. Dr. Carlson, of Regina, and Dr. Mulhern, United States foot-and-mouth disease specialist, on clinical examination diagnosed the disease on Monday morning as foot-and-mouth.
The herd is located six miles south and five miles east of Ormiston, Saskatchewan. The livestock involved is made up of twelve cattle and one hog. There is one contact herd belonging to a neighbour in which there are ten head of livestock. There are very few animals in the district, and no other contacts have yet been established. The burial pit is being dug today and slaughter is planned for tomorrow.
It has been reasonably established that the disease was transmitted from the area where it was originally found. May I say by way of further explanation that Ormiston is located five miles almost straight west of the southwest corner of the quarantine district.
How far is that from Regina?

It is about fifty miles
straight south of Moose J aw.

Since the new outbreak is just a few miles from where I live, may I ask the minister what effect this will have 
on the opening of the Ormiston P.F.R.A. pasture, which normally takes about 2,500 head of cattle?

The hon. member probably knows that this question was under consideration last week-that is, whether stock would be allowed into the pasture out of the buffer zone immediately adjacent to the pasture. At that time it was thought that probably stock would be permitted to enter the pasture, but I doubt very much whether stock will be permitted into the pasture now.

I have a further question. Will the government assist those farmers in obtaining whatever local pasture there is, and if there is not pasture available will some other compensation be made in the way of provision of feed supplies?

The authorities who are taking care of the situation there will, I am sure, give every possible consideration to the matter. There are other pastures, and some of them are so located that stock probably could be put in them from that district; but that is a matter which would have to be handled entirely by the men who are in charge of control of the disease.
Is this the case to which the minister made reference yesterday in his speech to the Rotary Club in Ottawa?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 8, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know what the answer is to the applause from the government benches.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Silence.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One answer, of course, could be not to make a speech at all. Such an answer might be very effective so far as this house is concerned, but one always has the hope that what one says may attract some small attention outside the house.

I shall, therefore, go ahead with the speech. As I proceed I very much doubt whether I shall have anything like the feeling of good will surrounding me that prevails at the moment, or indeed as large an attendance. I will say that if the intention was to make it extremely difficult to be critical, I shall strive to resist it as well as I can.
There may be some good things about this budget, Mr. Speaker, but I have not been able to think of any, except a few cases where the minister repaired mistakes which he made last year in spite of the warnings that we then gave him.
So far as I can find, my feelings are widely shared throughout the country. When I spoke on April 8 I said that the taxpayers of this country were becoming tax-angry, and the last two weeks have convinced me that I did not exaggerate. In choosing the date for his speech, I presume the minister thought that by throwing the remainder of the debate over until after the recess there would be a cooling-off period; but I am inclined to think he will find that actually there has been a bit of warming up.
The following extracts from the press, a few of which I shall read briefly, I think will go some distance toward indicating what I mean.
The Hamilton Spectator that well-known independent paper says:
If Mr. Abbott ever again has to perform the income tax sleight-of-hand he achieved on Tuesday's budget we suggest that he let us know in advance so we can get in the mood for it.
The Globe and Mail, in more serious vein, says:
He (Mr. Abbott) has had time to study the government's need of revenue for its three major spending activities, administration costs, social security plan and the defence program, but in none of these categories has he given any evidence of relating fiscal policy to either the means of taxpayers or the ends to be served.
I myself have felt that to be one of the great difficulties confronting us now, and I propose to say a little bit more about it later.
The Toronto Telegram says:
Douglas Abbott has bewildered the public by his juggling of the personal income tax rate.
I doubt if the minister realized quite what a job he was doing two weeks ago tonight.
The Calgary Herald refers to the minister in very spirited language, as follows:
It can be said without fear of contradiction that Mr. Abbott makes most vaudeville magicians look clumsy. His hand is indubitably faster than the eye . . . With a casual wave of his hand he can shrink an elephant of a surplus to half size in a twinkling. And when he places a glittering gold piece in the palm of the little guy in the audience, he is not content like ordinary magicians just to
22, 1952
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell make it disappear. He not only gets the gold piece back, but he simultaneously extracts a few nickels from the little guy's back pocket.
I do not know whether the minister recognizes himself in this guise, but the feeling is very widespread.
Then, again in more serious vein, the Ottawa Journal quotes-Mr. Muir, president of the Royal Bank, as questioning whether the government was justified in raising "such vast revenues". I think that is a thing that bothers us all, Mr. Speaker. It quotes Mr. Muir further as questioning whether the large amount slated for defence might not be spent this year and thus another large surplus be realized. That also is a question that I think is in many people's minds.
I have noticed a great change of heart. First of all the press showed an inclination to say: well, whatever we criticize, we must not criticize defence or defence production. That inclination has been abandoned and I think people are now looking carefully at this $2 billion and feel that we need to know a great deal more about it.
L'Action Catholigue raises a far-reaching question which really goes to the root of the matter. It says:
If the federal government has so many taxation powers that it prevents the provinces and the municipalities from functioning normally, this certainly goes against the spirit of the fathers of confederation.
L'Action Catholique gives an illustration, and a vivid one, of what it means. It goes on:
On the 28th of March of this year, when the municipal budget of the city of Quebec was brought down, Alderman Mr. Henri Beaupre said:
"During the last few weeks, we did everything we could to cut down the estimates-"
That is the estimates of the city of Quebec.
"-in order to be able to make both ends meet and during all that time some administrators in Ottawa were sweating in their efforts to find means to dispose of a huge surplus. Is that not enough to ask ourselves If there is not something wrong with our taxation system?"
In the light of what has happened, it is not surprising that these questions are being asked. As I said, people are warming up, and I think they should be warming up, because what is happening is that we seem to be getting back-in the lukewarm or cold war- to something like the war conditions that we had a few years ago when we spent over fifty per cent of our national income on war measures. The percentage is smaller today, of course, but on the present basis, say $4,800 million, as I said before, expenditure will amount to $13,150,000 per day, $547,000 per hour, nearly $10,000 per minute, or, putting it differently, $343 for every man, woman

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell and child, or $1,715 for a family of five, and, taking a rough figure, about $30 per week in taxation.
We can see that in spite of ourselves we are drifting back into the position in which we were in wartime, and we can also see that in wartime there was-and inevitably so-a great deal of government domination. We can remember also that at that time an enormous percentage of the business of the whole country was carried on by government, that the government was the great source of business to individuals, the great source of contracts; and of course the persuasive power of that huge amount of spending gave the government a tremendous hold over the people. I think it is fair to say that in retrospect we can see that in wartime we had not a few of the characteristics of the total state, and this could recur, if we are not watching it, in what I call a lukewarm or cold war.
There may be those who profit from government contracts and who think this is a pleasant state of affairs, but on the other hand I think critical voices will become more and more critical, as they are doing in the United States; they will realize and point out that the government's taking over industry is not the only way by which socialism can come; that we can have virtual socialism by reaching a stage where the government has taken such a large part of the whole income of the country that they would have unlimited power, or virtually so. The "point of no return" is hard to fix, but it is interesting to point out that even now taxation has become the biggest industry in the country so far as income is concerned. If we take the federal taxes at $4-8 billion, that amount is greater than the total value of all manufacturing in Canada in 1950, which was $4,378 million; and it is nearly three times as great as the value of agricultural production that year, which was $1,792 million.
As the Winnipeg Free Press says, these are appalling figures. They are appalling figures, they should stagger us, and they are staggering people and making them think about the cost of government as possibly they have never done before.
There are three questions I should like to ask and attempt to answer. First of all, is all this expenditure really necessary? Is there no hope of retrenchment anywhere? In my opinion the answer is that not all of this expenditure is necessary and that we should press for retrenchment to the point that we get it.


The second question is: Can the Canadian economy stand the strain? The third question is: What is the effect of the present high taxation on our people?
As to the first question-is all this expenditure necessary-I am going to leave it until later. I will deal now with 
question No. 2-can we afford it? My trouble is that there is nothing in the minister's speech which asks that question. I find no attempt to say whether we can afford it or not. In our private affairs when we make commitments we have to try to reckon up whether we can afford them and how we are going to meet them. But apparently in government affairs that is not so. I have no doubt that members of the government will agree that there is some point at which expenditures would become too heavy for free institutions, some point at which, in spite of ourselves- and without any intention of doing so, if you wish-we would slip virtually into a collective state, a socialist state, with freedom gone. But at any rate I say that the question, can we afford it, has not been answered by the minister; indeed, so far as I can see it has not been seriously asked.
There are some people who try to work out a formula. There is an economist, an Australian, I believe, who is called Clarke, who has tried to fix the danger point, which he says is 25 per cent of the national income; when you take more than 25 per cent, the danger signals are up.
As I said a moment ago, the point of no return is very difficult to fix. The only answer we get from the government is this. The attitude of the government seems to me to be inevitably the answer of the restaurant keeper in the southern states, who, in those dim days when pies sold for 5 cents apiece, asked a dollar for a piece of pie, and when the customer expressed outrage, the answer was: "Stranger, we need the money." I have a feeling that that is about the only answer we can get now.
What is the effect of the present situation on our own people? Well, we know the usual answer. The usual answer is to picture to us the tremendous capital investment, the increase in G.N.P.; and then we have pious admonitions that we should be thankful to live in such a country and under such a government, and we are told to compare ourselves with those who are less fortunate -and indeed, of course, most of the world is less fortunate. But, as 1 said the other night, there is not much satisfaction to many of our taxpayers to hear these millions and billions bandied about-they do not live in

a world of millions and billions; they live in a world of fives and tens, and less than that. It is the ordinary taxpayer that I am interested in, and it is the ordinary taxpayer that this house exists to protect.
As I said, many have done well out of inflation and currency debasement, and I regret to say that some of those who are doing well out of it seem content and practically say: It is not hurting me; I am getting by, and why should I worry? Before I sit down I want to suggest that we should all be much worried about it, not merely because many of our fellow citizens are so greatly affected, but because, if it goes far enough, it may ruin us all. But at any rate, our duty is to protect our people, and at the present time a great body of them are suffering.
It is always good to get an outside view of your position. In the Atlantic Monthly for May I ran across what struck me as an interesting and unusual assessment of our Canadian situation. Most of what comes from across the border seems to me to have not very much thought behind it. They seem to be dazzled by figures of investment and gross national product; but here is a statement from a responsible periodical which certainly tries to go to the mat. I quote from it briefly:
The dominion government, which last year anticipated a surplus of $30 million in a budget of S3 [DOT] 7 billion, found itself embarrassed by a whopping surplus that exceeded $500 million.
The minister will have to look into this, Mr. Speaker, because apparently they have not heard the news that the surplus is not $500 million; it is some smaller figure. The minister, I am sure, will observe this figure. I continue with the quotation from the Atlantic Monthly:
If Canadians were living through the most prosperous year in history it was certainly a queer kind of prosperity that nobody enjoyed. It was a twilight hazy kind of thing that fell rods short of everyone's notion of what prosperity should be like. Employers faced with cost of living statistics caved in before demands for higher wages. Prices kept rising.
The article goes on:
The combination of pockets of unemployment, agrarian discontent, and a continued rise in the cost of living made trouble for the Canadian Liberal government.
The article concludes:
More than likely Canadians are destined for more of the things they experienced last year-
I should have said that they pointed out the American investment in Canada, and then the article went on:
More than likely Canadians are destined for more of the things they experienced last year-higher
22, 1952
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell wages and less real income, more jobs and more unemployment, greater farm income in dollars and less to show for it at the end of 1952. And if all this adds up to prosperity, Canadians at the moment would as lief try something else.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not asking people to accept that statement as necessarily the last word, but I would state without hesitation that we do have in this country, despite our glowing figures, those grandiose figures, uneasiness, and the feeling that we have been on the crest of a boom year after year, and there is the fear that one day the boom will end and the reckoning come. Perhaps some people remember the old song no bird ever flew so high it didn't have to light.
The Atlantic writer was of course speaking of those elements in the community best able to take care of themselves, wage earners with a cost of living bonus, and that sort of thing. What he would say about the position of those of our fellow citizens whose income is still related to the dollar before its debasement, our citizens who have had no protection against the inflationary storm, but have had to bear the full fury of the blast-what he would say about them is hard to imagine. But what it means is that in spite of our fortunate position, which we talk about so much, in spite of our great natural wealth, we are out of balance, rather grievously out of balance. And of course one great reason, to which I shall add a word later, is the inflation of our currency by what the Winnipeg Free Press calls government profligacy of expenditure, as well as by other things.
I have tried to provide a background against which we can assess government tax policy, what it has been in the past year, and what it is proposing today. A year ago the government increased sales, excise and income taxes. We pointed out that this would increase prices. I give an illustration. Washing machines before the budget speech last year sold for $159.50; after the budget speech for $184.50. Before the speech, sales and excise tax on washers were $5.91; after the budget $20.30. Take toasters. The price before the budget was $9.95; the price after the budget was $10.95. The tax before the budget was 98 cents; the tax after the budget $1.50. There is not much room for doubt as to what happened there.
The fact was that the taxpayer got hit again and again. The higher taxes, instead of being deflationary as the government predicted, raised prices. Taxes went up; prices went up; national revenue went up, and of course the minister in a way is a beneficiary of it all, because his revenue went up and his surplus went up.

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell
The feelings of the taxpayers who were taxed so heavily were keen enough. But, to add to their distress, the taxpayers, groaning under the minister's exactions, watched with amazement and irritation the surplus which had been estimated at $30 million grow in nine months to $722 million. If the minister, when he spoke on the air in February, had contented himself with explanations, even if the taxpayers had not accepted his explanations entirely, they might have had sympathy with him; but the minister took a very different line, a very bold line. He said the surplus was a fortunate thing. He said he was pleased that he had taken several hundred millions more than were necessary, and he must not be surprised if the impression grew not only that the surplus was welcomed, but that it was not entirely unexpected. And of course when the Prime Minister also said it was a fortunate matter, that strengthened the impression.
Here are some excerpts from the Minister of Finance's words, taken from his radio broadcast. He said:
it-
That is, the surplus.
It has been an excellent thing, not only for the government but for each and every one of you.
He was talking then to the citizens of Canada. Again he says:
We had to use $300 million of our budgetary surplus to meet non-budgetary expenditures-
And that means the loans, advances and investments.
-leaving about $400 million of the total surplus available for paying off a part of the national debt and increase in our working cash balance.
Later on he says:
Supposing we had not had this large budgetary surplus. Where would we have got the money for all these necessary loans, advances and investments?
Then he goes on to explain that the money would have had to be borrowed.
In other words what the minister told us in February last was that in April of 1951 he did not provide for these other expenses, which he now takes care of out of this unexpected windfall.
But, secondly, and even more surprisingly, in his broadcast the minister said, while warning us that the surplus might be reduced by the end of the fiscal year, that he had spent virtually all the money in the surplus, that he had used virtually the whole of it.
The minister's comment on that was that it was used for purposes which had been approved by parliament. No one of course suggests that the minister had misappropriated the money, or that the money was not used


for things which in themselves were useful. But that does not alter these following facts:
1.	That the minister in April last did not provide in his budget for the items which he took care of out of this unexpected surplus.
2.	That he told us that he had used virtually all of the $722 million and-
3.	-and this is important-that this amount will have to be replaced; and there is only one place to get it, in the end, and that is out of the pockets of the hard-pressed taxpayer, who will have to find roughly $700 million more than he would have had to do at this time. Or, to put it differently, if this money had not been used by the minister it would have been available at this time of peak expenditure to give some relief to the taxpayer.
Instead of this, the taxpayer's money has been used for various loans and investments which need not have been taken out of the taxpayer's dollar, and also for the paying off of debt, which is good in itself, but which should be done according to plan and not because a blunder has been made in budgeting. That is the position; and the taxpayer will only get his money back indirectly and over the years.
In the circumstances, it is not surprising that there is confusion and indignation, wide confusion and indignation and that the taxpayers still believe that to this extent they were taxed unnecessarily in the last year.
I just mention this in passing, because I am sure the minister would like to have it on the record, that in a recent cartoon he was shown as a juggler making the surplus rabbit disappear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Unfortunately I cannot put a cartoon on Hansard. But the title I gave to it can be placed on Hansard, namely Abbott's Rabbit. I am sure that will be remembered for a long time.
So much for last year. I now come to the minister's proposals for this year which, if I may say so, are introduced with a mixture of well-assumed self-satisfaction and well-disguised repentance. When he said, "I feel justified this evening in saying that our policies have proved to be wise and right," I could not help asking: Is this the man who has already gone into reverse on so many of the things he did only a year ago?
And, to point up the irony, the very next sentence contains a really devastating argument against his own words, because in that sentence he said:
Events show that the inflationary virus in our bloodstream-

I think that is a good phrase.
-has taken a stronger hold than I had anticipated and that the prices increases that occurred before our measures took full effect were about five per cent greater than the forecast on which the budget was based.
Now, where does the minister think this virus came from? We told him where the virus was coming from; that it came out of his own taxes imposed last year. He did not have to be a clairvoyant to see that. Anyone could see what was going to happen-and what did, in fact happen.
I come back to the phrase "wise and right". Was it "wise and right" to retain the sales tax? Of course the minister seems to have a fixation on the sales tax, and refuses to admit his error. Or is he keeping it there in order to keep prices up and add to his revenue?
"Wise and right"-were the excise taxes of last year, which raised prices and caused unemployment, wise and right? The only wise thing was to abandon them. The minister, of course, gives high-sounding reasons for introducing them a year ago, ignoring completely the criticisms we made. And he now says:
We can ill afford much loss of revenue and I have given much personal study to this question. In this I have been helped by a considerable number of carefully prepared and thoughtful briefs from consumers, dealers and manufacturers. I am satisfied that a lower tax will now meet our reauire-ments.
I think the minister might have been generous enough to give us some of the credit for his change of mind. The truth is that the course of events, which we accurately predicted, has proved too much for him.
We now come to the cigarette tax-another mistake. The minister said:
In the case of cigarettes, I had forecast an
*C*fase	'"'-lion and I experienced a decline
of $1 million.
That does not seem very wise and right However, we will agree that the minister recognized that he had received a "knockout" and later he said:
I therefore propose, effective immediately, to move the cigarette tax back to where it was a year
If he had applied the phrase "wise and right" to his actions this year, instead of last year, we might have been able to go along with him. I am sure in due time the minister will come to the point where he will be much more ready to accept our advice, and not to delay it for a year. Because to delay for a year often causes trouble.
I now come to the income tax reduction. I was going to call it trivial, but you cannot call a thing "trivial" which does not exist at all. Actually when you include the social
22, 1952
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell security tax-which, after all, is the same kind of money, and comes out of the same pockets-it results in a $12 million increase.
Of course we realize what a difference an election year makes. It is interesting to go back to 1949, when the minister had a surplus of $410 million. Of this he "translated into tax reductions"-and that is a nice phrase, so I shall repeat it-he "translated into tax reductions" $323 million. But at the same time the minister gave this assurance, one which I think should be bracketed with the modest statement he made the other night, that the government had "carried through a program of tax reduction such as no parliament has ever made before, here or anywhere else." Well, that is an expansive phrase from an expansive minister on the eve of an election. I suppose we have not time this afternoon to carry the study far enough to make sure whether we can find a greater reduction. At any rate we realize why it was made then. And I point to the fact that this year, with a surplus practically as large, the minister has given virtually no tax reduction at all.
Then, as to the corporation tax. Of course we need not spend more than a minute on it. Everybody knows that 52 J was lowered to 52. The question is whether the minister, who told us how much he disliked the corporation tax, had any feeling of discomfort when he watched this surplus roll up, a surplus based so much upon taking taxes from corporations, taxes which he himself admitted were unwise.
No one knows better than the minister what a disaster it will be if, by reason of taxation, corporation earnings begin to shrink, so that his tax returns will begin to shrink-and there are some indications, which we certainly hope will not prove true, that corporation earnings may not survive the tremendous onslaught made upon them last year. And this, of course, is another reason for urging the need of retrenchment.
Then, we come to the income tax changes. We need not spend more than a minute on them, because already they have been laughed out of court by the public.
The minister, after his cat-and-mouse game of April 8, went on on April 15 to make another statement. I think the only comment one could make on that is that those who followed the vagaries of the surpluses, beginning at $722 million and then ending up at $356 million, would say that they are prepared for anything. Of course, in so far as the taxes which were over 100 per cent are concerned, they have been remedied. That is something which should never have been

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell done a year ago, but obviously it should have been set right. We hope that there is no catch in it.
There will be criticism of the apparent discrimination against people with smaller incomes. If we compare the income tax rates, including the two per cent for social security, we find that for the first half of 1952 with the new rates, in the case of a taxable income of $1,000 the taxpayer will pay $10 more; in the case of a taxable income of $2,000 he will pay $16 more; in the case of an income of $7,000, he will pay $20 less, and in the case of taxable income of $10,000 he will pay $52 less. From there on the disparity increases.
Just one further word as to corporation taxes, which of course are making it most difficult for new businesses to start up, something which we are urgently in need of. Also a word to remind ourselves that corporation taxes of necessity go largely into prices.
There is one other thing I should like to point out. Repentance is a good thing. Of course when you repent of a sin you oannot repent of all the things that have happened by reason of your actions. The minister's repentance cannot relieve the sufferings already caused in this last year. We must remind ourselves that the taxes last year were not imposed mainly on luxuries but were on household necessities such as stoves, washing machines, and so on, with the result that those who were establishing homes either had to pay the extra1 prices or do without.
Even now the trouble is not over, because when the tax reduction was made the other day it hit many merchants who had articles in stock on which they had paid the old price and in many cases they will be unable to recover.
Nor should we pass this item without dealing with the aspect of unemployment in the electrical appliance industry, which makes washing machines, stoves, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners, and many other electrical articles. In January of this year employment was only 52-6 per cent of January 1951, and production was 40 to 45 per cent of January 1951. The figures would have been lower still except that the industry, hoping for better days, had continued to manufacture beyond their needs and to increase their inventories.
I was quoting from the Atlantic a little while ago. The Atlantic was concerned with those who were in the best position to protect themselves. If they had been dealing with those people who are really the victims of inflation no doubt they would have spoken much more emphatically than they did. I wish now to say a word about those victims of inflation, partly because I think there is
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1
great danger of their being forgotten, and partly because I think it is most desirable that we should still be on our guard against further measures of the kind which have already debased our currency.
These people that I speak of are experiencing the sad truth about inflation, that it makes the rich richer and the poor poorer. It is not too much to say that there is widespread havoc among certain elements in the community who have no means of protecting themselves. We know who these people are who tare being victimized. In many ways they are the backbone of our country. They are the people who have sought to provide their own social security by means of personal savings, insurance policies and what not. They have tried to provide for their own old age and the security of their families.
Consider the case of those who are living on the benefits of life insurance policies or under wills. Take the case of a widow whose husband has saved so that they might live decently and educate their children. These are the people who have depended on what I would call the honest dollar. All these people have been betrayed. I do not mean intentionally; I mean by the unwisdom of the policy which has debased our currency.
You have only to take the case of people who were persuaded by propaganda in the last few years to buy government bonds on the assurance-it was virtually an assurance -that three per cent government bonds would not go below par. Those words were not actually used, but they came very close to it. I will read what was said, because I think we should keep these people in mind. Many of them have suffered; many of them have seen their securities go down almost ten points in some cases. That is the extreme case. Here is what they were told by a prominent and respected official of the Bank of Canada:
Government bond prices reflect the level of interest rates. A decline in bond prices could happen only if interest rates were to rise. In my opinion the needs of the future will require and enable the kind of monetary policy which has brought about the current level of interest rates. Continuation of this policy means stability in victory bond prices.
If the English language means anything that was virtually saying to these people that their three per cent bonds would not go below par. I think we can probably feel that the salesman, having been given a statement that went ninety-nine per cent of the way would not have much difficulty in going the extra one per cent. To me the amazing thing is that a statement like this could be made. It could only be made by one who believed in the omnipotence of the financial

authorities-that they were going to be able to maintain this rate and that there would be no change. It is wise for us to remember that, because nothing could show more clearly what happens to people who enjoy almost dictatorial powers in wartime.
It is no exaggeration to say that those whom I have described, those who depended on the steady value of the dollar, have taken the rap. They are really the people who are carrying the heat and burden of the day.
Let us consider for a moment the position they are in. Their goods cost more, nearly twice as much. The money which they invested is worth less today. This would apply to money invested in an insurance policy. The three per cent they receive on their victory bonds is worth only about one and a half per cent on the basis of the 1939 dollar. When the bond matures and the $100 capital is paid, it will be worth only about $50.
It is interesting to remember that the people holding these bonds will get $3 interest but in effect they have lost ten per cent because during the past year prices have risen to that extent. Do not forget also that these people pay taxes. It is therefore no exaggeration to say that these people are suffering dreadfully.
There is one other thing we should remember-that nothing has been done in any way to relieve them. It is a difficult problem, but we must bear in mind that many other people have the benefit of cost of living bonuses or wage or salary increases. Professional people have increased their fees, but these people are left, as I say, to take the rap. The government should never be allowed to forget the part which inflation, owing to the policy of debauching the currency, has played in this. It is the same as when kings used to clip the currency.
I believe it is essential to recall this. Serious people should be trying to remind their fellow citizens of this because it seems to me that little attempt has been made to help these people. I know there are a great many-I know some personally-who practically take the line: I am doing very well and I am not going to worry yet. These people should not forget the history of currency during the last twenty years and realize that if inflation really gets out of hand it will ruin everything. Another reason I think it is important to emphasize this is that we have no guarantee the government will not resort to inflation again. After all, at the present time members of the cabinet are not seeing quite eye to eye. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) says

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We will say a small rise. On the other hand the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) tells us there is good reason to believe that the thing which sent the cost of living index up last year now is working in reverse. I suggest the ministers get together and tell the same story.
It is useful to have a realistic picture like that in the Atlantic Monthly, because we get so much rather indiscriminate praise from the United States, usually from people who have made rather a mess of things themselves. I always think it is a little like the pot calling the kettle white.
Now I come to the question I reserved. Is all this expenditure necessary? A year ago when the minister placed before parliament his estimates for this year he foresaw a reduction of $35 million below last year. That seems a long, long time ago; and of course it was only a few months until that hoped-for reduction was replaced by an increase. I suppose if the minister felt free to do so he would say, "We should not have promised retrenchment and at the same time put on taxes which shoved prices away up," but that is a hard thing to expect the minister to say, and I certainly would not expect him to stand up and say it now. We sympathize with the minister in his task, or rather we would sympathize with him if it were not that all our sympathy must be reserved for tne taxpayers.
As I said before, we are in danger of getting back into a semi-war atmosphere where economy is outmoded. The other evening I quoted the rather strong words which had been used by that great government supporter, the Winnipeg Free Press It spoke about government profligacy, which means wild and unrestrained expenditure. That is a strong word, especially coming from the mouth of a friend. What I am afraid of is that we are back in a war atmosphere again, and I am a little afraid that the familiar phrase uttered some years ago by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) may have infected the whole service.
I propose to refer just briefly to a few items which seem to me to rather stick out. There is an item of $46 million for travelling and removal expenses. I think that might easily stand some investigation. Of course it includes the cost of transportation to Korea and Germany; but as I recall those figures they

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell are not staggering in themselves, and would still leave a very substantial portion of this $46 million for other purposes. It seems to me there has been an awful lot of moving around. The impression I get from those who have more to do with public servants than I have is that years ago if a public servant were going to travel, a certain amount of formality had to be gone through. You did not just do it all on your own. I understand now it is very much easier, and they are apt to descend upon one like a cloud of locusts, not just one person but that they travel in very considerable numbers. I should think that item would bear investigation.
Then, of course, we come to our old phrase, and what wonderful words they are: "Publication of departmental reports and other materials. Films, displays, advertising and other informational publicity." I find those words hard to pronounce, but we all know what they mean. They really mean that the public gets a certain amount of information and the department gets a certain amount of advertising. I should think it would be about one for the public and two for the , department. Well, there we have these millions of dollars; yet I find that is not quite the whole story, because that figure does not include some of the people in the departments who get paid for working on publicity. It is very hard to find out how much of a man's time is devoted to publicity and how much to other things. It is very difficult to press that beyond a certain point of inquiry, but I do think this matter would repay investigation.
There is another thing which interested me very much and which I think will interest all people, particularly those who are not economists, as I am not. I think the ordinary man would be interested if he knew there were a dozen or fifteen departments of government each with its own economics department. External affairs, for instance, has 15 economists; agriculture has a staff of 125. As compared with those we are almost relieved to find that the finance department, where one would expect to find economists, has many less than the Department of Agriculture. Finance has only 24. I think that department had better buck up; it is being left away behind. In the labour economists research, branch we have 141. I have not added all these figures, but if that were done I am sure we would get a very imposing total. Whether there are fifteen branches of economics, I do not know. Whether economics in the Department of Agriculture is different from economics in the Department of External Affairs, and whether that again is different from the
economics in the Department of Labour, let us say, again I do not know. But it would seem to me there might be some sort of central bureau anyway.
I remember being given this bit of advice years ago when I was in business and a small new department was being set up. My wise chief said to me, "Now remember, that means you are going to create a new king, and he will want to have as many subjects as possible." So I think when you have similar branches in fifteen departments you are bound to have a lot of overlapping.
Well, now we come to national defence. I want to make some comments later on about the big, broad figure of $2 billion, but there are some other matters, trifling in the face of $2 billion, I would like to mention first. Here is a figure that interests me. Apparently national defence spends $4,891,000 on telephones, telegrams and other communication services. This seems to me to stick out like a sore thumb, when we recall that after all almost any part of Canada can be reached by air mail within 24 hours. It seems to me you could send an awful lot of telegrams and other information and make a lot of telephone calls for $5 million; and I would have thought a good deal of the information could have been supplied by using Her Majesty's mails, royal or otherwise.
Now I want to say just one thing about the Petawawa incident because it calls up something we in this party tried to do, with an utter lack of success. When we learned that quite apart from military personnel nearly 40,000 civilians were employed one way or another in the Department of National Defence we urged that some kind of expert assistance should be brought in to organize this huge enterprise. Well, we got the brush-off, as we in the opposition are accustomed to getting the brush-off; but the explanation was very unconvincing. I remember being told that efficiency firms could not deal with anything as big as this, that they could deal only with small companies. As it has turned out, that was just 100 per cent wrong. Now we have this incident which apparently makes it perfectly clear that it would have been wise if the department had taken our advice at that time, just as it would be so wise if the Minister of Finance would take our advice from time to time. At any rate here we have a splendid instance of locking the door after the horse has been stolen. Apparently the minister has known for some months that things were not good, but of course we could not expect him to tell us. Now he is getting Mr. Currie from Montreal to investigate, and a most competent person he is. I hope Mr. Currie's investigations will cover a lot of territory.
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1

Just as one small straw to show the way the winds can blow I should like to mention a little incident that took place in the defence expenditure committee last autumn. It came to my attention that an invitation had been sent out to tender for 63,000 serving forks. The man who got it felt that this was a strange request, and he sent it down to me. I made some investigation about serving forks, and I found that a serving fork is apparently something which is used at a formal dinner where the waiter comes along and takes meat from a platter with this special fork to put on the guests' plates. I was told that a large hotel might need a score or two. I would not have imagined that in any military mess, outside of the officers' mess, there would have been a large number of serving forks used. I have had some experience with military messes, and I believe it is mainly a case of rugged individualism there; everyone looks after himself. I must say that this number of 63,000 was questioned and the defence department did reduce it to 40,000, but apparently there was still no doubt that they wanted tens of thousands of serving forks.
I produced this serving fork at the committee. I took great risk because I carried it in my pocket, and it extended out in such a way that if I had fallen I would have injured myself. I did, however, at great personal risk to myself bring this fork into the committee. It was presented there, but so far as I know no action has been taken.

speechtext: At the committee meeting this morning a statement was tabled showing the number to be 14,000 and not 40,000; action was taken.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I congratulate you. I do feel that this is progress. The number was reduced from 63,000 to 40,000 and now down to 14,000. If we strike off a few more zeros we may get it down to somewhere near the right figure. Speaking seriously again, this is a case where obviously something incredibly foolish was done. The action was questioned, and it seems to me if there had been any efficiency in the organization at all they would have jumped on it in a second. They would have found at once what a foolish thing was being done. If there had not been some complaint we would apparently never have had this figure reduced to 14,000. All I can say is that the more one hears about this matter the worse it is. I am not going to risk my life by taking this fork around any longer, but I hope the department will do something about it. A colleague points out to me that there is now one fork for every five men.
22, 1952	J481
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell It may be that we now have such refinement in the service that the men are going to wait upon each other, and perhaps they will need these serving forks.
Perhaps this case affords some explanation of another thing. It is not surprising, if there is a need for 40,000 serving forks, that the department needs such a large number of civilians to look after these things. It turns out that in the defence department we have something like 23,000 permanent and temporary civilians, and in addition something over 14,000 casual civilian employees. This figure represents about 20 per cent of the total of all the rest of the civil servants in all departments including the post office. I do not know how it strikes hon. members, but at least to me it suggests the need for careful inquiry.
I come now to the $2 billion figure for defence and defence production. I want to make some comments on that. I think it should be fully explored. I want to make it clear that in this party we wish to make an all-out effort on defence. There is no question about that, but that is not to say that we should mechanically assume that the figures given to us are the final word in economy. We must inquire into that.
What about the defence department itself, I mean the personnel? We have been given the picture of the multiplication of officers, and how well we know that picture! One instance in Calgary was cited where a staff was sent in at an estimated cost of $50,000- the minister did not question that in his reply-and the work was done .by a colonel and several other officers. If I recall correctly the work had been previously carried on by a reserve officer and some N.C.O.'s at a suggested cost of well under $1,000.
We should not expect men in the services to be interested in expenses, Mr. Speaker.
I think we would be naive to expect that. It is not their job, but the job of parliament. As a matter of fact, we ask the man in the service to provide us with protection. I have some knowledge of the army and I would think that anyone who expects military officers to be careful about the money they spend is naive to an extreme degree. Add to that the fact that most of the officers got their training in the recent war and you realize that, as those of us who have been in the army know, when a country is at war the idea of having regard to the money cost of what you are using is rather remote. Being of a thrifty nature myself, and tainted with a certain amount of Scottish blood, I did try to look after government property as well as I could, but I was regarded as something
1482	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell in the nature of a lunatic. This is not the job of the officer, it is the job of parliament.
To whom do we look? The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton)? He is completely surrounded by the spenders. He has to be in the hands of his technical advisers. As I said, their business is to strengthen defence and not to ask how much can be spent to strengthen it; that is our job.
We come now to the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), and he will understand the way in which I am using these expressions. I think his history is very much the same as the history of these military officers in so far as money is concerned. He is inoculated with the same virus; he is a kind of war baby, too. He blossomed and flourished in wartime. In those days he had all the money he wanted. The question was not, "how much will it cost?" but "can we get it and how soon?". Therefore, we must not be surprised if he talks in an offhand way about large sums of money which, however important they may be to the rest of us, seem to him rather like the small dust in the balance. How can he worry about the odd millions? He has other things on his mind, and that may be one of the reasons that he was $284 million wrong in his estimates of expenditures during the last fiscal year. I should like to refer to that because in the defence expenditures committee we had somewhat of a close-up of one or two items which gave me an understanding of the difficulty which faces the department. This experience also made me feel how foolish we would be if we regard the figures which are shown to us as ascertainable and well established figures.
I am going to read a little bit of the evidence given at the meetings of the defence expenditures committee last December. We in the opposition would have liked to go a little further with the inquiry but the committee was shut off on December 13 because we had to begin getting ready for Christmas! -although some hon. members will recall that we were here beyond that time. The civil servants were extremely co-operative in getting us the information and I want to make it clear that what I have to say is no criticism of them. Nevertheless, the results were profoundly disappointing. They certainly made one feel that estimates were little more than guesses.
Mr. Mackenzie, the deputy minister of defence production, in discussing construction contracts said:
The estimated values that are given are in some instances too low, although it is not yet possible to revise those estimates in any firm way.


Mr. Harkness then questioned Mr. Mackenzie as follows:
Q. What do you mean by estimated values there? As I understand this you have a list of the contracts that have been let. A. That is right.
Q. That is not an estimate is it? A. The first column of figures in each case is the estimated value of the contract.
Q. In other words, these are not firm contracts then? A. Oh yes, these are firm contracts.
Q. I mean, as far as the total amount is concerned? A. Many of these contracts do not state a firm price.
Q. That is what I mean-I should have said a firm price. A. We have had to estimate what the ultimate cost would be.
Later, Mr. Mackenzie said:
Some of the contracts are as I said in my earlier statement cost-plus contracts, where we do not know at all what the ultimate is going to be.
Later, questioned by Mr. Wright regarding purchases of howitzers:
Q. And for the United States government there is an item of 38 105mm. howitzers, with an estimated value of $1,457,646. Approximately the same amount of money is being paid for only 88 of these howitzers bought from the United States government as compared with $1,500,000 for 138 of these howitzers being paid to Sorel Industries Limited. Might we have an explanation for that?
A. This is just an illustration of what I was saying, that the estimated values can be very misleading. The 88 howitzers were being bought from the United States government and that is the estimate we got from them on what we would have to pay. That is not a firm contractual price, that is an estimate which was received at the time. Now in addition to buying 88 howitzers from the United States, it was decided to manufacture this particular type of howitzer in Canada and it was thought at the time that the order would amount to one and one-half million but whether that will prove to be the case only time will tell.
Q. Then these figures do not really mean very much?
A. I was particularly careful to say that, when talking about these orders for equipment that are being made for the first time in Canada, it is practically impossible to be categorical as to what the items are going to cost.
Q. You will notice that there is a vast difference in these two items. A. It may well be.
Q. It would look as if they could be made much cheaper at home than brought in from outside the country.
A. It may well be that the purchase from the United States will not amount to as much as that, or it may well be that the cost of manufacturing them in Sorel will be higher.
Mr. Speaker, I draw attention to the fact that this is not an order for some new type of radar gadget which was just invented the day before yesterday. I suppose that howitzers are 50 years or 60 years old. This order is for the manufacture of howitzers.
Hon. members will notice the utter vagueness of the figures which are given. Apparently they are not contracts. They are
__what shall I say?-expressions of intent.
Yet with vague figures like that, I presume, we have built up this figure totalling altogether $2 billion.

There is one other item that I should like to mention in passing, namely the item of $213 million for the acquisition of land and the construction of buildings in Canada. That amount apparently is in addition to the $311 million spent for that purpose last year. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) mentioned that matter and raised the question whether, in these times when we are so greatly extended, we need to spend this huge amount. The gossip, of course, is that we are going to have our own Pentagon building all dressed up in modern fashion, underground and all that; that is the talk. One wonders whether these expenditures have to come. If we were as far astray as $284 million in 1951, heaven knows where we will be in 1952 with the larger figure.
In this same Atlantic Monthly from which I read I was interested to note one or two things from the United States experience which I should like to mention briefly. Speaking of waste in military procurement the Atlantic Monthly said:
A decision to change the design of a plane or tank when production is under way can cost hundreds of millions of dollars.
An efficiency drive is in progress there and two instances of what they have done are worth mentioning. The secretary of defence who is an active fellow, whose name begins with "Mac", has reduced catalogue items carried by the armed forces from 15 million to 1-5 million. Another interesting incident is that they have discovered how to manufacture a certain part going into an airplane, which formerly cost $2, at a cost of less than one cent. The Atlantic report goes on to say: The real elimination of waste will come through a combination of constant probing plus consistency in policy decisions.
These illustrations from the United States should be useful in two ways. First, they should make us doubly and triply critical of all estimates put before us; and second, they should give us great confidence that economies can be made if those who are spending the money are forced to make every effort to find them.
Mr. Speaker, the situation in which we find ourselves reminds me greatly of the situation of a year ago. We then had before us a surplus estimated at $30 million; now it is $9 million. Having regard to the huge amount involved, they are both what you call nominal surpluses. At that time we reminded the minister of the surpluses, so unexpected, in the years past. The total for the five years is $1,970 million. Nothing the minister has said to us this year makes one feel that this might not happen again. I read to you, Mr. Speaker, the shrewd comment of Mr. Muir of the Royal Bank who was not born yesterday and who suggests what I am sure many of us thought, namely that the surplus for next year may be in the $2 billion. There is a lot of room for economy in $2 billion. I have indicated some soft spots, and I have no doubt that there are a great many more.
There is one other consideration which should not be overlooked and that is that it is not reasonable to suggest that a minister who may quite well be facing an election next year has stripped himself of all hope of a surplus, with 1953 as a possible election year. After all, let us remind ourselves again that there was $284 million shortfall in defence expenditures last year. For these and other reasons I think it proper to ask again and again that retrenchment should still be sought, particularly in this $2 billion, and that we may still have hope for a reduction in these appalling expenditures.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"the proposals of the Minister of Finance are unsatisfactory because they would continue to levy excessive and unjust taxation instead of assuring substantial tax reductions.
This house condemns the government for taxing far beyond actual requirements and for its waste and extravagance.
And this house regrets the failure of the government to assure efficient administration in all departments of the public service."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in following the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) I do not propose to cover quite the same ground, but in several respects I shall underline some of the points that he made so ably in the course of his remarks. When I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) introduce the budget my mind went back to the first budget which was introduced in 1936 after my election to the House of Commons. That budget, including interest on the national debt, loans to our

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell railways, and every other expenditure of government for the year 1936-37, amounted to *approximately $530 million. The budget now before us, again in round figures, amounts to almost $4,300 million or approximately eight times as much as the budget which I heard introduced by the Hon. C. A. Dunning in 1936. Both of these budgets were peacetime budgets. And what a strange twist of fate it is that in this period of peacetime the Canadian people should be called upon to raise, one way or the other, the enormous sum of $4,300 million. Of course the levels of the income cannot be compared, they are so different. At the present time we are spending over $2 billion for defence, defence against external aggression-and I am not complaining of these expenditures so long as they are carefully made, and so long as they are necessary, but I would point out that we had grave internal dangers in 1936, with hundreds of thousands of people on the verge of starvation or of want, with young men herded in relief camps getting 20 cents a day, and people being sent out to the backwoods of our prairie and other provinces and receiving allowances amounting to as little as $6 a month for a family. In other words, we can find, when we have to do it, money to protect ourselves from external aggression, but apparently we cannot find money in other times to protect the people of this country from the burden of poverty, of misery and of want such as they experienced during those fateful years between 1930 and 1939.
I could not help but think of these matters and make this contrast when the minister delivered his budget speech the other night. While I am going to criticize what he said, once again I think the drafting of the statement he made, his speech and the manner of delivery left nothing to be desired. I think that we could follow it intelligently and understand what the minister was saying, although at times he seemed to be saying quite contradictory things.
First of all, I want to agree with the hon. member for Greenwood when he said that the minister, in bringing down the budget, spoke as though he were actually effecting a reduction in personal income tax. Indeed, in describing the new change in the income tax structure, namely, the incorporation of the 20 per cent surcharge tax for defence into the regular taxation rate, the minister said this, as reported at page 1254 of Hansard:
I expect the revenue loss as a result of these changes to be about 6 per cent in a full year and this loss in revenue is a general indication of the average gain to the individual taxpayer. In other words, the average taxpayer will pay 6 per cent less than he would otherwise have done under the income tax law as it now stands.
[Mr. Coldwell.l
However, a comparison of the 1952 tax rates with 1951 rates will soon show that the minister's statement was, in my opinion at least, entirely misleading. It is true that by incorporating the 20 per cent surcharge into the regular tax structure in the manner in which the minister has done, we shall pay in a full year, beginning this July, approximately 14 per cent instead of the 20 per cent we would otherwise pay under the existing law. But the minister has found it convenient to overlook the fact that the full 20 per cent defence surcharge has never yet been imposed. Last year, for example, we paid a 10 per cent surcharge, and now by the minister's indicated change we shall pay roughly 17 per cent for 1952 and 14 per cent in the full year commencing in July.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

But different calendar years.
I still say this cannot be considered as a reduction in the sense that the Minister of Finance used the words. What the minister has done is to use the originally imposed 1952 defence surcharge tax of 20 per cent instead of the actual 10 per cent surcharge tax figure in effect up until the end of 1951 in his comparison of the 1951 tax rates with the tax rates for 1952.
The changes in personal income taxes are therefore deceptive, for while they ostensibly reduce income tax, in reality they have the effect of increasing them. For example, a single person with an income of $2,000 last year paid $165 in tax. This year he will pay $175, or an increase of $10 before the social security tax of 1 per cent is levied. And in the same way a married taxpayer with no children and having an income of $3,000 paid $165 last year, but will, under the new changes, pay $175, exclusive of the social security tax. I think this demonstrates very clearly that our income taxes have been increased over the 1951 rates before the social security tax is included. The minister has, however, given the impression that if it had not been for the social security tax the income tax rates for 1952 would be lower.

speechtext: I would like to stress another point-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: No.

speechtext: Well, it is.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; the increase I have shown is before the old age security tax is imposed.
I would like to stress one other point before
I leave the subject of income tax. It is with regret that we learn that the minister has imposed a heavier tax increase on the lower income groups than he has done in the case of those in the higher income brackets. For example, a taxpayer who is married and without children and earning $3,000 per year -and that is the same category-has had his over-all personal income tax for 1952 increased by 12 per cent over his 1951 rate. On the other hand, a taxpayer who is married and without children, and receiving $20,000 a year-earning $20,000 a year, I should say-finds that his taxes have risen only about 6 per cent above what he paid in 1951.
I say that is hardly fair. Certainly it is not a fair way of allocating the burden of raising government revenues, if it is to be on an equitable basis, and on the basis of ability to pay.
It is interesting to note, too, that our criticisms of the so-called 2/2/2 formula introduced at the last session of parliament for the purpose of financing old age security become more than ever justified in the light of the minister's indicated sources of revenue to pay for this pension. Let us look at the sources of revenue that will be tapped in order to pay for this social security.
The minister has estimated that the 2 per cent sales tax allocated for this purpose for the present fiscal year will yield $135 million; that 2 per cent of the taxable personal income will yield another $52 million; and that 2 per cent of corporation income will produce an additional $48 million. This adds up to a total of $235 million, and leaves a deficit therefore of roughly $87 million necessary to finance out of general revenue to meet old age security.
Last autumn, when the old age security bill was before parliament, we of the C.C.F. criticized those features of the bill which imposed the flat rate of 2 per cent on the taxable portion of personal incomes, with a maximum payment of $60 a year; and we criticized, too, the 2 per cent on corporation
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell incomes. At that time we pointed out in particular that contributions could only be made equitable if this maximum of $60 were removed and a graduated tax on personal incomes levied for this purpose.
If that had been done, not only would the social security tax have been made more equitable, and consequently more fair to all concerned, but there would have been less than $87 million to be made up from the general revenue. As it now stands, 42 per cent of the amount necessary to finance this pension must come from the sales tax, which is a particularly oppressive tax for the lower income groups to bear. We have said that before, and I wish to repeat it. We see that 16-1 per cent is to be derived from personal income tax and only 14-9 per cent from corporation tax levies, with the remaining 27 per cent to be derived from the general revenue.
Indeed, if we examine the manner in which the personal income tax for assisting in the financing of old age security is apportioned, we find that this tax lies most heavily on those in the lower income groups. The house will remember that last fall we of the C.C.F., as well as others in the house, criticized the unfairness and discrimination of exempting from this tax that portion of a taxpayer's income above his taxable $3,000. This means that the burden of financing this program falls upon those with taxable incomes up to $3,000 a year, to a greater extent than upon those with more than $3,000 a year of taxable income. Above this income tax level the tax stops with individuals paying the maximum of $30 for this year, whether they make $10,000 or $100,000.
I say it is disappointing that this unfair apportionment of income, together with the sales tax out of which most of the money will be found for financing this social security program, will, as I have noted, cause the cost of the program to bear most heavily upon the lower income groups, and the middle income groups, which in our opinion are at the present time quite hard enough pressed.
The minister's abolition of the 15 per cent excise tax on various commodities imposed by the last budget, and the reduction from 25 per cent to 15 per cent on other commodities, are in themselves to be commended heartily. However, as the hon. member for Greenwood indicated, putting these taxes on one year and taking them off in the next points up the grave injustice which has been inflicted upon those who furnished their homes last year. I wish to say to the minister that this shows either incompetence

The Budget-Mr. Coldvoell or the governments disregard of the needs of the people who must furnish their homes in this highly inflated post-war period.
The Minister of Finance has once more demonstrated the government's disregard- and I wish to emphasize this-of the expressed wishes of the House of Commons by his failure to remove the four per cent floor on medical expenses. Just two weeks prior to the introduction of the budget the House of Commons unanimously adopted a C.C.F. resolution, moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), which in effect would permit taxpayers to deduct from their incomes before computing the amount of income tax to be paid the aggregate of their medical expenses, rather than only the portion in excess of four per cent of the taxpayer's income, as now provided in the act.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister should not lose his temper. I have not lost mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
