The question of whether or not we can afford to undertake these projects does not seem to come up for examination until they are reflected in our annual estimates.
I think that attitude of mind has been proven, Mr. Speaker, on a good number of occasions across Canada. I want to make this point. I am not this evening speaking of the Department of Defence Production. I have no hesitation in saying that I think Canada has been most fortunate in having as deputy minister of the Department of Defence Production Mr. Mackenzie who, from all accounts, has done an excellent job for this country. I might say at this time that
The Budget-Mr. Herridge I think it is most unfortunate that the public service of this country is in the near future going to lose his services to private business.
I think that attitude on the part of the military to plan extravagantly without concern about the cost to the taxpayer, to plan elaborately, or as this statement says, "to undertake projects that do not seem to come up for examination until they are reflected in our annual estimates", has been indicated on a number of occasions. I think the minister will know that on a number of occasions across this country the Department of National Defence has indicated the necessity for a certain building and then the tenders to construct that building have been too high for the money provided. Then the Department of National Defence has had to trim its sails a bit, do away with some of the frills or some of the unnecessary things, and finally the building has been constructed at a cost within the estimate and has proven quite satisfactory, and sufficient. '
I want to be quite fair. I think the situation is rapidly improving, from what I have been given to understand; and I think the present minister has done a great deal to improve the co-ordination between the different branches of the various services of the Department of National Defence. But in my opinion there is no question that there is still a certain amount of interdepartmental jealousy that prevents the best of efficiency, and that is not to the advantage of the taxpayer or of the defence effort as a whole.
Even the Industrial Preparedness Association mentioned this fact in its bulletin of April, 1951, and at the same time said that the army was being starved for the benefit of other services. I understand that the Industrial Preparedness Association is an association of manufacturers working together with a view to securing some efficiency in the production of defence needs. You do not usually expect them to be critical of defence procedures; but in that bulletin of April, 1951, even they were critical of this aspect of the administration of the Department of National Defence. To indicate further that there has been interdepartmental jealousy and some lack of co-ordination, I want to quote as follows:
At the air force's 25th anniversary banquet in Ottawa on April 1, 1941, a former chief of air staff, Air Marshal I,. S. Breadner, publicly deplored the fact that the navy had infringed on air force priority in the air, and said of the decision: "It is ridiculous-absolutely ridiculous. Air forces the world over are not too well recognized even yet. The other services have not given up the fight to subordinate us one iota.'' The next day an embarrassed government official said that Canada's navy would continue to invade R.C.A.F. skies "whether Air Marshal Breadner likes it or not."

I think that this house must insist on intelligent co-operation and planning between all the services, regardless of the jealousies that may arise from latent traditions, priorities and things of that sort. We must insist on intelligent co-operation and planning in this department if we are to get value for the taxpayer's dollar.
I have quoted a few excerpts and given a few illustrations of the opinions of persons in important positions in the Department of National Defence. Before proceeding I want to quote one more person's opinion on matters of defence, an opinion that is respected in this house and in the country, an opinion of a gentleman with a long and excellent record as a professional soldier, and with an excellent parliamentary record. I refer to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). I find that on page 2810 of Hansard of May 8, 1951, the hon. member for Nanaimo said:
I have never known an admiral, a general or an air marshal who did not begin by asking for more than his share of anything.
Who speaks with better experience in this house than the hon. member for Nanaimo? To ask for more is a natural failing. Perhaps some of us practise it in other directions. But who should know better than the hon. member for Nanaimo, and to whose advice should we listen more than to the hon. member for Nanaimo when it comes to speaking from experience in military affairs? This attitude mentioned by the hon. member for Nanaimo, and attitudes indicated by other statements I have mentioned, show a state of mind that spells waste and unnecessary expenditure of the taxpayer's money, unless it is arrested by the supervision of the minister's senior officials, by constant vigilance and by the greatest co-ordination between the various services.
This waste and unnecessary expenditure are caused without doubt, on the evidence of what has happened recently at Petawawa, by lack of satisfactory and adequate supervision, by lack of co-ordination, and without a doubt by the state of mind that I have mentioned, which has little regard for the cost of this service to the taxpayers; by the state of mind that fails to remember from day to day that this money is provided as a result of the work and the toil and the sweat of the producing and working people of this country.
Well, I have attempted to give some evidence to prove that waste and lack of coordination exist. I wish to give one or two illustrations of the state of mind that I have been talking about, the state of mind that I would say illustrates a complete lack of understanding of the working of the processes
	|

of democracy, of an understanding of the principles of government economy, and an understanding of responsibility to the Canadian people. The incidents I shall mention will be trifling in some instances, because this department is different from other departments. As I said before, it is different from the Public Works Department, where you can go and look at the wharf and see what you got for your money, or where you can go and look at the public building and see what you got for your money. Because of the necessity, and the proper necessity, for secrecy in some respects in the Department of National Defence, and because of the innate nature of the expenditure and the purpose of the expenditure, it is very difficult for a member of parliament, or for any person, to detect the expenditures of the Department of National Defence and be at all certain that the people of this country are receiving value for their money. It is on that account, Mr. Speaker, that I maintain that the heaviest responsibility, so far as public expenditure is concerned at this time, rests upon the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), and also because of the vast amount of expenditure and the peculiar nature of the department which he is called upon to administer.
I frankly admit, Mr. Speaker, that we all recognize the minister has a very heavy task, and that he has been working long hours for many months. We give him credit for that, and any suggestions we have to make from this side of the house are not made in a harping or critical spirit, but they are made in an effort to be constructive and co-operative in the administration of this department.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, the average member in this house, or the average citizen, has little opportunity to deal with big things, and in fact, in many respects, he is not competent to do so. But sometimes small events, small incidents, indicate a state of mind, as I said before, the direction in which the wind blows. I am going to bring to the attention of the house a few things that have come to my notice in travelling about this country, and I trust that in his examination of the situation the minister will continue to do all he can to stamp out this state of mind and to arrest its development. This is the state of mind that I mean, that does not consider the public purse. I got on a train once, a branch line, meeting a main line train. This is not recently. A colonel got out of the drawing room on the main line track and got onto the branch line train. The branch line train had no chair car. It just had two day coaches. He arrived on the train and he said to the conductor: "Where is the chair car?" The conductor said: "There is no chair car on this

train, sir. You have to sit in this coach." In the coach there were the ordinary working men and their wives, the ordinary people of Canada. Well, this self-appointed nobleman straightened up and said "Impossible! I am not going to ride with these people." And he got off the train and he telephoned, and this country paid for a car to travel forty miles along a road parallel to the railroad because this gentleman was not going to ride in an ordinary day coach twenty miles to his destination. I just use that as an illustration. I am not suggesting that there are large numbers like that. That is the type of man who is not concerned with the expenditure of the people's money and does not understand responsibility in the real sense of the word.
I was coming to Ottawa for a session, and the train stopped at a prairie city for 40 minutes. Like most people, I got out of the train and walked around the station. I went to get back about twenty minutes before the train left. A C.P.R. constable was standing there. He said: "I am very sorry but you cannot get on. They are switching sleeping cars, or something." So we stood there. In front of me was a lady with a baby in her arms. Along came a brigadier and he said: "Stand aside, please." So the lady with her baby in her arms stood aside, and he went on to the platform and got in a coach. I said to the C.P.R. constable: "Why did you let him through and keep the mother with her baby in her arms standing here for twenty minutes?" He said: "Sorry, sir, that is orders; he is a brigadier." That shows a complete lack of democracy and of the things we stand for.

The Budget-Mr. Herridge the train I thought that I would see where this gentleman had placed himself. I found he had a drawing room although he was going only a hundred miles. I do hope the minister will do everything possible to check that sort of thing, because, while the amount involved may be small, it does bring about considerable public irritation and does not improve our defence effort.
I should like to deal with another matter brought to my attention because, while it is only a minor thing, it does indicate a lack of thought for the expenditure of public money. I was talking to a permanent army sergeant who is to be retired at the end of this year. This man told me he was going on a course which would last six months. I said, "What for?" He said, "It is a course in modern weapons", to which I replied that I thought it was a useless expense. Here was a man who was approaching 21 years of service and was being sent on a six months' course on the latest type of weapons, with a view to instructing others in the use of those weapons. Surely it is not in the interests of economy to give a course to a man who is about to go on pension. The giving of the course would have no value to the Canadian taxpayer, because in a short time this man would not be in the army. I mention this to show a lack of consideration for the taxpayer's dollar. When I mentioned my view to the man he said, "Well, why should I worry?" I had told him that I thought it was a totally unnecessary expense. However, I did not tell him who I was because, as I said before, I like to travel incognito.
All this indicates that there has to be a determined drive from the top to have some persons realize that this money is the taxpayer's money, and that it should be spent to the best possible advantage. I have every respect for the minister and his deputies. I believe his deputies are striving to do their best, and, while possibly under some handicaps, are making every effort to improve the services.
Then, I would pay my respects to a number of men I know who are serving in the reserve army. I know some good officers and men who are giving their evenings, and some considerable time in the summer, to assist in the reserve army, and I am convinced that they do not receive the credit they should. Those men give careful consideration to expenditures, and are trying to

The Budget-Mr. Herridge carry on with limited equipment, and with a view to developing a corps which can give service to this country.
I was greatly impressed recently by the keenness shown by some young engineering officers, and the concern they showed with respect to expenditures, and what equipment would cost. We have large numbers of those people in the services, and I pay my respects to them, to their efficiency and their integrity.
While it is our right and duty to criticize, I must say that in this country we are very fortunate, when we stop to compare the situation in this country with that in the United States.

Mr. Speaker, there are two matters I should like to place briefly before members of the house. The first is one which I have brought up on other occasions during the past few years, the serious erosion of the shores of our great lakes. On February 12 of this year an important meeting was held at the Brock hotel, Niagara Falls. This was attended by municipal authorities and land owners along the shores of lake Ontario from Niagara-on-the-Lake to Toronto and by members of the Lake Land Development and Beach Protective Association Incorporated of New York state.
After considerable valuable discussion it was decided that the two governments should be petitioned to take immediate action. As far as the United States end of the business was concerned, the United States department of state approached the Canadian government on February 22 requesting that this matter be brought before the international joint commission. According to press notices of the following day the Department of External Affairs stated that this was not by any means the way to deal with this matter, that it should be dealt with in some other manner concerning which so far I am a bit in the dark. I have requested that correspondence between the two governments be produced but so far this has not been done. Sometime in the future we may learn the true picture.
Most certainly this is an international matter, it is not one for Canada to deal with alone. This business of passing the buck between the province and the dominion in connection with lakeshore erosion has been going on for the past seven or eight years. I feel that this matter is of such vital interest to Americans and Canadians living along the shores of our great lakes that it should be taken up by the international joint commission. I am unable to understand why the Canadian authorities did not agree to this when they were approached by the state department.
The Budget-Mr. Lennard
When the opportunity arises later this session I shall probably have a great deal more to say on this serious matter of lake-shore erosion. It is a serious matter because people are losing their homes and farmers are losing their fruit land. The great Niagara fruit belt is gradually being worn away, as I have stated before. Nobody seems to care very much about it as far as our governments are concerned, and I am referring to the provincial as well as the dominion government.
Another matter with which I wish to deal momentarily this evening will also likely receive attention later on. I think this calls for some answers from the government. Sessional paper 18A was brought down as a partial answer to some questions which I had asked this session. One question was:
How many contracts for defence footwear were let from April 15, 1951. to February 29, 1952?
I also asked the amounts of the contracts, to whom they were let and at what price.
I did not secure all the information that I desired because the return does not indicate the number of pairs of shoes contracted for, simply stating the amounts of the contract, the different firms to which contracts were let with the amounts, and the total amount.
At the present time the total number of our armed forces is under 100,000, and that would include all men, women and children. The total of the contracts awarded for footwear in this ten-month period was $15,292,241.70. I do not know whether members of the armed forces are provided with walking-out shoes, combat shoes, mess footwear, dress shoes and all that sort of thing, but if the shoes were contracted for at a cost of $15 per pair that would mean over one million pairs of shoes for the 100,000 personnel in our armed forces. That is over ten pairs of shoes for every man, woman and child. I include children because some of the contracts were let with baby footwear companies.
I think it is the duty of the government to inform this house as to the number of shoes contracted for in this period. I regret that I did not ask for the contracts let in a longer period but I thought that my questions would provide the information I desired. I think it is the duty of the government to provide this house with detailed information in respect to this huge quantity of footwear contracted for during that ten-month period, because to me that seems enough shoes to equip the armed forces for the next six or seven years at the present rate of enlistment.
As I say, my questions were not fully answered, and I would ask that the Department of Defence Production look into this matter a bit more thoroughly. I also understand that this answer merely indicates the

The Budget-Mr. Gillis amount of leather footwear procured for the armed forces, and does not include the rubber footwear also contracted for during that period. If the whole picture were shown, the amount might be far greater than is indicated by these contracts.
In conclusion I repeat that it seems to me an expenditure of more than $15 million to equip our armed forces with footwear, when they number well under 100,000, is exorbitant. This would seem to be just one more indication of the lavish way in which these defence contracts are being let and have been let for several years past.

speechtext:
Before I begin to talk about the budget I would like to say a few words in reference to what was said by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and others in regard to defence expenditure. When the present defence set-up was discussed in this house I, along with others, argued that no one man in this country could handle the business of national defence and look after the interests of three departments, the army, the navy and the air force; and I have not changed my mind. Any man who tries to do that job, I do not care how brainy he is or how strong he may be physically, is not going to last very long. Anyone looking across the house at the present minister will realize that he has been asked to carry a load that has just about got him down.
When this set-up was being discussed I argued that at least there should be another minister, a minister for air. We are practically back to where we were in 1940. We are starting to re-organize our air force on a new basis, and judging by the recruiting campaign that is going on it is not going to be a small force. No minister can handle those three departments, check and sign the requisitions himself, and determine whether or not the money is being spent wisely. We did not get much support for our suggestion that another minister be appointed. Three deputy ministers were appointed, however, and they are doing a good job. They can handle the correspondence, but don't forget that when decisions are made or large requisitions come in, the minister has to look at them and decide. He has to make all the decisions; he also has to run around the country doing the inspecting and so forth.
At that time we suggested that a defence committee be set up in this house; not the public accounts committee, who merely take a look at the public accounts and try to check expenditures and so on, but a competent committee of this House of Commons. In my opinion such a committee should have [Mr. Lennard.l
been sitting, dealing with defence expenditures only as they are made from month to month. I believe such a committee would have been very helpful to the minister; and it might have helped prevent the sort of thing we are seeing at Petawawa. That leaves a pretty bad taste in the mouth of the average man who is paying high taxes. He does not object to paying high taxes if he knows he is getting something for them; but when he reads the sort of story that came out of Petawawa the average man is led to believe that instead of organizing an army, spending your money wisely and doing a patriotic job, you are just setting up a gangster machine which is in there to get everything it can for itself. It is pretty bad, and I hope the situation will be cleaned up soon.
However, I have no intention of taking a whip and starting to beat the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). I have a fairly good realization of what he is up against. I know it is not humanly possible for any one member of this house or any one man outside this house to go in there and do the kind of job that man is expected to do. The sooner the government smartens up and realizes that more help of a ministerial nature is required, the sooner we will get away from this gangsterism that is going on in connection with the unwise spending of our money. I still think that defence committee should be set up in this house. It should be meeting continuously and examining national defence so the house would be assured the money was being spent wisely, and kept informed as to the plans of the department.
I got up primarily to talk about the budget. Whether or not we agree with the minister,
I like to see a job well done; and I do not think any member can deny that when the minister presented his budget he gave one of the best exhibitions of footwork I have ever seen in this house. I think that was the best speech he ever made, and I compliment him on it. He was right on the bit and was inspired that night. I admire a good job, whether or not we agree with all the minister said. It was pretty hard to catch him out then, but we have had a lot of time to think it over since.
I am not going into the facts and figures the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) dealt with this afternoon. I do not like to duplicate a job done by somebody else. To the extent that he could pull something out of the mess of words the minister put on the record, I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar did an excellent job of showing that taxes were not lowered but that in fact in the over-all picture there

would be an, increase this year. The hon. member showed that the budget was not popular and was not an election budget. But it is a good let-down now tor a build-up later on, and that is not bad strategy either. I believe the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made a good case this afternoon, and I am not going to duplicate it. We gave him the job of giving the main talk, and I think we should leave it with him.
However, I should like to say this on the question of medical expenses. I believe the minister slipped up a bit there. I believe that floor should have been taken out altogether. It seems to me a person should be able to charge all his medical expenses, and that there is a great deal of discrimination in the application of that feature of the budget. For example, in upping the ceiling the minister did give relief to the person who is able to go to the Mayo clinic, and who can write a cheque for a couple of thousand dollars. If you can go to Dr. Penfield and write a cheque for a couple of thousand dollars, you get some relief under the change made by the minister. However, by leaving that floor in the act the person who can merely take care of ordinary medical expenses gets little relief. In a lot of industries throughout this country there is a system of paying the doctor and the hospital by the check-off, just as you pay your taxes. In my end of the country that system has been in operation for a good many years. It is a group system whereby the doctor is paid $52 a year and there is a subscription rate for the hospital of $52 a year. This $104 is paid as an insurance, and perhaps 50 per cent of the people who pay it never receive any benefit from it because fortunately they have no sickness. They pay in order to help the fellow who is sick most of the time. Out of an income of $1,600 or $2,000, that $104 per year is a heavier burden than the $2,000 for the man who can write that cheque and who receives exemption for it under this new regulation.
If the minister had removed that floor and had permitted the deduction of the type of payment I have described for medical expenses-the system I am talking about only covers ward charges and there is an addition to that if you happen to go into hospital but at a lower rate than if you were not a subscriber-the ordinary man would have obtained some relief. I still think the minister should give consideration to that It is seldom that a budget is changed, but if the minister wants a good election budget next time he should remove that floor so that those in the lower income brackets who try to maintain some kind of insurance for
The Budget-Mr. Gillis themselves against sickness will be able to write that off for tax purposes.
There are other items that I should lit to bring to the minister's attention. Practically every business in this country is allowed to write off the purchase of new equipment or a Neon sign in so far as income taxes are concerned. These things can be charged to operating expenses. Commercial travellers can write off their expenses in travelling, and make certain deductions for the use of their cars. I should like to bring a specific case to the minister's attention. In this budget he has permitted the deduction of union dues for tax purposes, and that was welcome. I have had representations, and no doubt the minister's department has also always had representations from industrial workers on many occasions. I am going to take the coal miner as an example. He has to purchase his explosives with which he blasts the coal. This runs into quite an amount of money during the year. Secondly, he has to purchase a certain type of hat which he buys from the company. It is a hard fibre hat to protect his head and save compensation costs in the event something falls on him. In addition to that, he has to purchase a certain type of shoe with a metal toe-cap. Then, if a 180-pound machine falls on his toes it will not crush them but merely jam them up a bit. The explosives, the hat and shoes are the tools of the miner's trade. They are a part of the machine of production. It is necessary for him to spend that money and secure the equipment in order to produce coal.
If the merchant and the commercial traveller, all those persons doing business, are permitted for tax purposes to write off the money spent on expansion or improvement of their business, I do not see why the minister would not give serious consideration to permitting the coal miner to deduct the cost of purchasing that type of equipment. I am putting this on the record so that when the next budget is being prepared the minister can give some consideration to what I have said.
While I am on that point, I should like to say that democracy is never taken from you in one blast. It is slowly but surely chiselled off a little at a time. I was rather disappointed that the government did not give serious consideration to the vote of the house concerning deduction of medical expenses. I say that in all sincerity. I remember the vote of this house on the milk subsidy. Later on, it was changed by order in council. I remember that the veterans affairs committee brought a recommendation

The Budget-Mr. Gillis into this house that a half acre of land would be the requirement to come within the scope of the small holding section of the Veterans Land Act. This recommendation was accepted in the house and a short time after we left here, to my disappointment, the land requirement was stepped up by order in council to three acres, thus eliminating hundreds of applicants who would have qualified under the recommendation made by the veterans affairs committee. I am afraid that in this day and age, when the tendency is to usurp the powers of parliament as a government by the people, you are setting precedents, and if you allow that to continue you will arrive at the position where the House of Commons will be a place in which people can talk but not much attention will be paid to them. Slowly but surely the supremacy of parliament is being lost. It is a development that I do not like to see.
When there is a free vote in this house I believe the government is morally obligated to accept the results of that vote. If a vote were taken in most fraternal organizations or trade unions across the country, I do not think there is any officer or any executive who would for one moment consider that they could take action contrary to the vote cast by the membership. I am a little bit leery of this business of a small group like the cabinet taking the power unto themselves to say that the House of Commons did not know what they were doing when they voted. Three times since the end of the war that type of action has been taken, and I suggest that members on the government side, particularly the cabinet, stop and think about it. If that sort of thing continues there is not much use in the members being here. I want to leave that thought with the members of this house because democracy is chiselled off very slowly. For some considerable time I have seen growing up in North America, not so much here as in the United States, a kind of managerial society. They are managed from the outside. This business of not paying attention to what goes on in the house, and ignoring the votes of this house, is in my opinion a bad development. It certainly should be stopped by the members.
There is another item which I should like to bring to the minister's attention. I went through his budget speech and the resolutions, but it is rather difficult to find anything that you can get your teeth into. As I said before, the minister did a good job in presenting it. It is not popular in the country; but when you ask someone to tell you just exactly what is wrong with it, the only thing he can say is that we did not get a tax reduction but we got a slight increase. When you go over the 
budget, it is not easy to say what is wrong with it. It is generally the things that are not in it that you have to quarrel with.
On several occasions I have had correspondence with the department about allowing as a tax reduction the housekeeper of a person who maintains a home and who is obliged, through sickness-his wife being ill and in hospital-to hire a housekeeper. I have written to the department about the matter and I have a letter here in my hand-I am not going to read it-with bills attached, wherein this person showed that the cost of maintaining his home had gone up considerably because he had to hire a housekeeper, pay her wages and maintain her, and at the same time had his wife in hospital and was paying a hospital bill.
I figure that that housekeeper is a legitimate expense. In my opinion it is a more legitimate one than new equipment and that kind of stuff that is purchased at a plant. The home is a first requisite of the nation; without the home to hold you together as a nation you have not got anything. That man is struggling to maintain his home for himself and his family while his wife is ill. If you can write off the expense of maintaining your father or mother who may be dependent on you-and that is just a minor expense compared with the cost of maintaining a housekeeper, paying her wages and maintaining your wife in an institution-in my opinion you should be able to write off this expense.
I wrote to the department and I have a reply dated as late as April 16 of this year.
I am just going to read that reply because I think it is rather cold-blooded. It reads:
Dear Mr. Gillis:
In reply to your letter of April 7 on behalf of Mr. Fraser Goodwin of Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, you are advised that the amount expended by Mr. Goodwin for a housekeeper is a personal living expense of the taxpayer.
The Income Tax Act specifically provides that no deduction can be allowed from income for personal living expenses.
It is not personal living expenses at all. It is an abnormal expense that cannot be budgeted for. It is likely to hit you at any time, or it may never hit you. I agree that the person who wrote that letter for the director general of the assessment branch is correct when he says that there is in the Income Tax Act no provision for exemption for that particular type of expense; but I am asking the minister now to give consideration to perrhitting that type of deduction if and when he has the problem under consideration. Maybe he could bring in an amendment when the budget resolutions are up for consideration, and I strongly suggest that he should do so. This is the type of case that creates

a great deal of hardship in the home where a person with a small income is obliged to employ a housekeeper in order to maintain his home.
I have here another resolution, and no doubt the minister has it. It is from the office of the city clerk, Fort William, Ontario. It has been circularized all over the country. The copy that I have comes from Sydney, Nova Scotia, and it deals with that question of federal aid to education. I am not going to argue that question. It has been argued by several members in this house, through a resolution. I put my opinions on the record, and I stated that it is a matter of either federal aid or a revision of the tax agreements as between the provinces and the dominion. I am convinced that there is no way to solve the problem of the cost of education in this country unless it is centralized with the federal government and grants are made to the provinces, earmarked for that purpose, the administration being done in the provinces.
In this resolution it is suggested that the total cost of education in the country should be paid out of income tax. I am not particularly anxious about specifying what particular tax it should come from; I think it should come out of general revenue. I am bringing that matter forward again because it is a serious problem, particularly in the maritimes, and I hope that the minister is thinking about it when the new tax agreements are finalized, so that the provinces which desperately need aid may get a proper revision in their agreements until such time as some of the provinces who oppose federal aid smarten up and get around to the point of realizing that it is absolutely necessary.
I have quarrelled a bit with odds and ends, and I never like just to oppose without having something to propose. Tonight I am going to say a few words with regard to new methods of financing that I think are necessary. I have spoken before in this house on the same matter. The reason that I cannot quarrel so much with the minister over the budget that he brought in is that, following the methods of financing in this country as agreed to by most of the members in the house, he has to get his taxes in a certain way and he has to spend them in a certain way; it is the orthodox method and it has to be carried on in that way. When the Industrial Development bank was proposed in this house I think maybe I was about the only one in the house that opposed it. I opposed it on the ground that it was just another adjunct to the chartered banks, that it was never going to mean much in the development of this country, and that it was an organization that was being set up to 55704-96
The Budget-Mr. Gillis underwrite doubtful investments. I said that it would provide some plant expansion but that it would create no new industry in this country. That has been the history of it since it was set up. In the maritime provinces the bank did not even establish an office. Anyone who could get a loan from that Industrial Development bank could get it through the chartered banks because he had to have collateral to back it up. As to creating any new industry, or as to being of much value in the creation of small subsidiary industry at least, the Industrial Development bank has not accomplished much.
At that time I suggested that, instead of an Industrial Development bank, what was needed in this country was a national co-operative bank, creating a new chain of finance. I am firmly convinced, and have been for a good many years, that changes are coming in the economic structure of North America, whether we like it or not. There is only one way in which you are going to expand democracy and hold onto it, and that is by giving the people of this country more ownership; by that I mean more ownership in homes, in financial institutions and in the development of the general co-operative movement. I have been convinced of that for a good many years. When a man owns his home he has his roots in the soil; he is a citizen; he belongs to the country and to a certain part of it.
There are thousands of credit unions across this country. They have developed a lot of brains in that field of finance in the way that they see it. They have amassed a lot of capital. The co-operative movement is today proposing-and I know that representation has been made to the government-the setting up of a national credit society to co-ordinate all of the credit movement across this country. They have been turned down on that application; but the time is coming, in my opinion, when it should be done. Just while I was home over the Easter recess I attended a meeting in the city of Sydney where the Sydney credit union-there are four of them in that city-with a membership of about 2,000 had purchased a new hall. It is fitted up like a modern bank. It is as good looking inside as any of the banks that I see in this city. It is modern in every way, and fully staffed. We had Dr. Watson Kirkconnell, president of Acadia university at the present time, there. He was the main speaker. Well, nobody can accuse him of being a socialist.
I just want to read a little bit about what he had to say at that meeting. Knowing the gentleman as well as I do, I was a little bit surprised to hear him express the views that
1514	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Gillis he did express at that gathering. In one part of his speech Dr. Kirkconnell had this to say:
Dr. Kirkconnell said one of the most notable features of the credit union system is the extremely small margin of losses through bad debts. In Prince Edward Island, for example, loans from 1936 to 1949 totalled nearly $1,500,000 and the uncollectable loans $1,041, a loss of one-fourteenth of one per cent. New Brunswick in 1946 reported loans written off since inception of $2,116, or one-fortieth of one per cent of a total of over $8 million.
The Sydney credit union was launched in October, 1935, and since that time has acquired 2,000 members and assets of slightly over $350,000. Since its inception it has loaned out $1,750,000 and during that time has written off less than $900 in bad loans.
That is only just one small credit union in that city where there are four of them. The island of Cape Breton has a chain of them. The province of Nova Scotia has a chain of them right across the province, linked up with a central credit union league in the province, where they are trying to arrange long-term loans. That is true in New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and clean through to British Columbia.
This is a new chain of finance, and what I suggested, instead of the Industrial Development bank, was to set up a national co-operative bank. This is not new. They have had it in Europe for years. The United States has a national credit union act today, similar to the one that the Canadian credit movement is looking for at the present time. If that organization was set up on a national scale, all of the credit unions across the country could be members of it. If shares were sold to the general public at anywhere from $10 to $100 it would give everybody in the country who wanted to participate an opportunity to become members of the new chain and use that co-operative money to develop small subsidiary industries across this country that you cannot find risk capital to undertake. If that were done it would, in my opinion, be driving the roots of democracy further into the ground by giving people ownership in the development of new wealth in the country. It would also help by setting up a yardstick for the chartered banks.
In my opinion the government annuities have done much to keep the old line insurance companies in balance in regard to their rates, and so forth. The government has already set a precedent by going into crown corporations. In my opinion Trans-Canada Air Lines would never have been developed if it had not been for government initiative and government money. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is another example and so is the Polymer Corporation at Sarnia, and also Canadian Arsenals and atomic energy, and now television. These are good examples,


in my opinion the best examples on the North American continent, because every one of them is successful. They were properly developed. In my opinion the government should give serious consideration to the request from the credit union movement across this country to set up a national credit union act to utilize the brains and the money that are now found in that movement, to give it proper national direction and assist in developing industry in this country that risk capital will not touch.
I hope the minister is listening, and I hope that he will give today's Hansard to some of his advisers, and check the whole matter, because the credit union movement has arrived at the position where it is demanding this. They know they are ready for it. I consulted them three years ago as to whether this kind of thing should be pursued, and they said they were not ready for it. But they are ready, and they made application for it, and they have been rejected by the government. Of course it may be that the government was not ready for the presentation because they had not studied the matter as well as they should. I trust that the government will give serious consideration to what I am talking about at the present time, because I think the time has come when we shall have to start giving the people more ownership.
I myself have never objected to the wealth that the big corporations had. What I have always objected to is the power they had to prevent the creation of new wealth by the people themselves. This credit movement now has sufficient capital at their disposal. They have linked themselves up on a national scale so that they can act for interprovincial purposes and develop small industry or big industry. It is a step in the right direction. It is driving the roots of democracy further into the soil, and in my opinion that is the only way democracy can plan, because you will go either backward or forward. A backward step is a step back towards fascism. Do not make any mistake about it; fascism or communism is not the product of any particular country; it is the product of a system, and the system being older in the countries where they capitulated to these ideologies is an indication of what can happen on this continent unless we smarten up and get more ownership into the hands of our people, give them some incentive and establish them as good citizens with roots in the soil of this country. In my opinion that is the only way you can continue to expand democracy. The only way it can be done is through that ownership as far down as you can get it in the proper direction.

I still think that the minister is not out of the woods so far as inflation is concerned. He has a right, a legitimate right, to ask me: Well, what do you think should be done. You do not think that we have got inflation stopped, and all that kind of thing. I am going to put back on the record what I think should have been done. We recommended this in the last budget and in the budget before. Before we are through with this business of inflation and deflation we are going to have to carry out this kind of program.
I believe there should have been a renewal of price controls with subsidies to bring down the cost of essentials. I believe that will have to be done sooner or later. I believe that there should be some regulation preventing any further general increase in rents. That is another scare to most of the people of this country who are renting homes. Go to Montreal, Toronto, or to any of the larger cities where rent controls are handled by the provincial governments or by the municipalities. They are not very effective, and there is a general fear of eviction on the part of our people at least once a year.
I believe you have taken some steps to prevent price fixing by monopolies, and I hope that this resale price maintenance will be followed up. It is at least bringing the rule of law for the first time into the field where most of the money of the average person is spent. We enact laws to prevent people from picking our pockets, robbing banks, slugging us on the street, hijacking, and all that sort of thing. But where 80 per cent of our money can be filched from us by inflated prices and crooked practices, we have done nothing. I believe that if resale price maintenance is followed up it will establish a rule of law -that will be respected by those who have been fixing prices and who have been robbing people indirectly in the past.
I believe the Winnipeg grain exchange should have been closed to eliminate speculation in foodstuffs. I believe it was LaGuardia who said some years ago, in discussing the possibility of feeding the rest of the world, that if he had his way he would close down every grain exchange in North America.
I believe in a wage program worked out with trade union representatives to help hold the price line, while assuring workers of a fair income, and I have stressed that time and again. I have said that each industry should have an industrial council which would meet with the Department of Labour, and that would have full knowledge of the economic picture, and what the continued demand for wages would mean in the field of inflation. I believe that an industrial coun-
The Budget-Mr. Gillis cil should have been set up right after the war, and in time we will have to get around to it.
Then, I believe in a minimum price program worked out with farmers' representatives, to ensure primary producers a fair share of the national income. The committee on agriculture does that to some extent, but I believe farmers would be more satisfied if they had direct representation.
Then, there are other measures such as credit restrictions, and the like. The government has already taken some steps in that direction.
In conclusion I would urge that the minister and his department take a look at the possibility of introducing a national credit union act. They should examine the movement right across the country, and get the facts and figures. Let them see the large number of people who, voluntarily and in their spare time, have studied this system of finance, through groups, and have perfected an organization second to none across this country today. Let the minister see if such an organization could not be advantageous to the whole country, if it was linked up on a national scale, so that interprovincial negotiations could be carried on for the development of the country and the benefit of small industry-and perhaps for big industry, too, because there is a considerable amount of money involved in it today.
I trust the time is not far distant when I will see the minister introduce a bill along these lines-because, if he does not, sooner or later I shall do it myself, and have a vote of the house recorded in connection with it.
